Rule 400 requires approved processing, post-processing confirmation, renewal reassessment, and a clear record of the facts, rationale, and authority for every endorsement attachment, revision, or removal; unaddressed endorsement issues must be referred before issuance.

The authority matrix requires referral of a requested water-backup limit above $25,000 and prohibits binding the referred request until documented approval; this is an internal authority threshold, not a contractual water-backup limit.

Rule 410 sets the Section I all-other-perils deductible selection floor at $500, requires the selected option to be supported by risk characteristics, and requires the selection to be documented; this is an internal underwriting floor rather than a universal policy deductible.

Rule 410 requires use of an available deductible for the applicable coverage part, prohibits inferring an unstated deductible or combining terms from separate proposals, and requires referral of conflicting, unavailable, unsuitable, or exceptional deductible requests.

Rules 410.M and 410.N require application of the available named-storm minimum and wind-deductible ceiling but do not state numeric values; the applicable contract and state overlay supply the actual parameter, and requests outside normal authority require referral.

Rule 410 requires deductible selections to be consistent with submission, rating, issuance, location, occupancy, construction, protection, property use, and cause-of-loss information, and prohibits using a deductible to offset unacceptable property conditions or satisfy premium preference.

Rule 410 requires current-information review for deductible changes, prohibits retroactive application and post-loss revision based only on claim information, requires capture of the final selection before binding, and requires completion of deductible review before issuance.

HO 04 90 (2027-01) is effective only when attached, preserves unmodified policy terms, and contractually applies a $1,000 deductible to covered water-backup damage from the same occurrence; Rules 400 and 410 constrain attachment and internal selection without changing that contractual deductible.

HO 23 74 (2025-05) leaves the applicable policy deductible in force and applies it after the endorsement's roof-surfacing adjustment; Rules 400 and 410 constrain roof-related attachment and selection but do not replace the contractual deductible or settlement sequence.

HO 23 77 (2022-07) contractually applies a 2% to 10% windstorm-or-hail percentage deductible based on the applicable limit, while Rule 410.N constrains internal selection to the applicable underwriting ceiling and Rule 400 constrains weather-related attachment without changing the endorsement's stated percentage.

Rules 600 and 610 are internal underwriting controls: Rule 100 prohibits using the Manual to alter coverage, and Rule 600 makes inspection evidence part of risk selection and file handling rather than stating a premium, deductible, settlement, or coverage result.

Rule 600 requires an inspection when underwriting information is incomplete, inconsistent, or unreliable and prohibits binding until the issue is resolved or an authorized exception is recorded; it also requires the trigger, information needing verification, and binding disposition to be documented.

Rule 600 requires a roof survey before binding when roof age reaches 15 years, with evidence addressing roof condition, materials, installation quality, and visible deterioration, and requires the reported age, request, findings, and underwriting action to be recorded.

Rule 600 supplies inspection or referral triggers across property condition, occupancy and security, structural and moisture concerns, systems and site conditions, premises hazards, business or construction use, prior damage, discrepancies, utilities, code notices, access limitations, conflicting external data, unresolved recommendations, and unusable photographs.

Inspection evidence must come from a reliable source with sufficient authority and relevant expertise; altered, incomplete, or unverifiable material cannot be relied on, and the file must identify the source, verification performed, evidence reviewed, and action taken.

Rule 610 requires underwriting to record receipt and verification dates, source attribution and limitations, and material discrepancies, and to resolve a conflict before completing action when it affects eligibility, classification, or terms.

Rule 610.AA says an inspection report is valid for “18 from its completion” but does not specify a unit; the completion date and use decision must be recorded, and unclear Manual direction must be escalated rather than converted into an invented validity period.

Rule 600 requires prompt review of inspection findings, referral of hazards outside normal authority, and no waiver of material conditions without authorized approval; Rule 610 requires the file to state the operational decision, basis, follow-up, eligibility findings, and authority used.

Corrective requirements must address a material inspection condition, state an objective required outcome, and identify due status and verification method; completion must be supported by reliable evidence rather than an unsupported verbal statement, with remaining concerns and closure action recorded.

The inspection process may close only after every material finding is resolved, referred, or accepted within authority, with final inspection status, outstanding conditions, authority applied, and final underwriting action preserved; withheld access, requested evidence, or material information must be documented and any adverse action must follow applicable procedures.

Rule 610 requires an audit-ready underwriting record that preserves material facts and sources, terminology, timing, discrepancies, decisions, referrals, conditions, eligibility findings, risk characteristics, inspection findings, authority, restrictions, adverse-action rationale, corrections, and quality-review resolution.

Rule 610 requires professional and factual notes, prompt recording of material actions, preserved correction history, and documented approval for departures from underwriting direction; Rule 600 requires inspection reports, photographs, communications, and related evidence to be protected in the underwriting file with access limited to legitimate underwriting purposes.

Rule 600 and 610 underwriting controls are separate from post-loss policy duties: the HO-3 form separately requires inspection, records, damaged-property preservation, inventories, photographs, examinations, and proof of ownership after a loss, and says an inspection before or after loss is not a representation that property is safe, sound, or eligible for coverage.

Rules 230–250 are internal underwriting controls for risk selection, referral, evidence, and acceptance; they must be applied before binding within delegated authority and do not alter the coverage grant in the issued policy.

A pending referral is not approval: the underwriter must hold the affected binding, renewal, change, or endorsement action, use an authorized recorded channel, and satisfy approval conditions exactly before acting.

Rule 230 requires referral for material premises-liability hazards including unsafe pools and water features, recreational and elevated structures, animals, weapons or explosives, business or visitor activity, rental or lodging, hazardous property conditions, and unresolved premises disputes.
Rule 230 requires a swimming-pool barrier at least 4 feet high and requires correction or acceptable control of damaged barriers and gates that do not close and latch securely before acceptance.

Rule 230 does not state a separate dollar authority level or numeric clearance period; its watercraft provision refers to an applicable outboard-horsepower threshold without stating the horsepower number, so the current controlling source must be obtained rather than inferred.

Rule 240 requires prior-loss review before accepting, renewing, or changing a risk, covering the preceding 3 years and including reported, paid, denied, and open property claims where available; applicant disclosures must be compared with approved loss sources.

Rule 240 requires referral of a risk with 2 paid property claims in the applicable history and prohibits binding without underwriting authority; its large-loss referral provision names a threshold but does not state the amount.

Rule 240 evaluates loss cause, recurrence, current condition, and repair quality rather than claim count alone, and requires referral when remediation or cause correction is unclear, including repeated water loss, unresolved roof or electrical concerns, and prior premises-liability hazards.

Rule 240 permits reliable repair evidence such as photographs, invoices, contractor statements, and inspection reports, but requires referral for incomplete, altered, or inconsistent evidence and does not permit binding while a required prior-loss referral remains unresolved.

Rule 250 requires verification of occupancy before binding or continuing, distinguishes resident use from seasonal, intermittent, nonprincipal, temporary, and unoccupied use, and requires prompt notice of a material change from owner to nonowner occupancy.

Rule 250 directs application of the vacancy condition when customary occupants and personal property are absent and states that vandalism is excluded after 60 days of vacancy; it does not provide a numeric deadline for its prompt-notice requirement.

The Manual's Rule 250 60-day vacancy position is distinct from DP-3 Rule 150.N, which separately states 30 consecutive days for vandalism handling; these internal product positions must not be presented as a new contract exclusion.

Rule 250 requires referral and verification for tenant, rental, short-term rental, home-sharing, lodging, mixed occupancy, detached-structure occupancy, subleasing, unauthorized occupants, and unclear possession or maintenance arrangements; rental review includes lawful access and landlord-contents ownership.

Rule 250 requires a final supported occupancy, vacancy, and rental classification before underwriting action and prohibits binding or continuing when reasonable inquiry leaves material occupancy facts unresolved.

Manual Rule 300 supplies general delegated authority ceilings of Coverage A through $800,000 for a line underwriter and through $1,500,000 for a senior underwriter, while the Texas appetite separately states a $150,000–$1,200,000 eligible Coverage A range; these are separate eligibility and authority constraints rather than coverage limits.

HO 04 42, HO 24 71, HO 24 73, and HO 24 82 provide distinct contractual liability or personal-injury grants only according to their attached terms; an underwriting referral does not change those terms and an attached endorsement does not automatically clear an internal eligibility or hazard referral.

HO 24 71 states a shared $100,000 limit for the sum of damages arising from business pursuits, while HO 04 42 limits its grant to a lawful incidental occupancy subordinate to residential use and not materially changing the residence character.

Rules 200, 210, and 220 are internal pre-bind and renewal underwriting controls for property risk selection, referral, holds, conditions, and documentation; they do not alter coverage, which remains governed by the applicable carrier-issued form, declarations, and attached endorsements.

Rule 200 requires construction information to be complete and classified by predominant exterior-wall construction, requires reliable protection-class verification, and refers unsupported construction, access, fire-water, and response information before final underwriting action.

Rule 200 requires a wind mitigation inspection before final underwriting action when Coverage A exceeds $750,000 and requires review of material roof, attachment, and opening-protection information when wind exposure is material.

Rule 210 requires roof inspection findings before binding at roof age 15 years or greater and holds binding authority until acceptable condition is supported; it requires decline at roof age 25 years or greater without discretionary override.

Rule 210 requires reliable evidence for roof age and replacement scope and refers deteriorated, damaged, leaking, inadequately repaired, materially worn, inaccessible, or otherwise unverified roof conditions; required corrections must be completed and documented before binding when necessary.

Rule 220 requires identification of water sources and prior water damage and requires referral of active leakage, moisture staining, mold evidence, wet materials, or unresolved water entry; binding may not proceed while the Rule 220.C condition remains unresolved.

Rule 220 routes plumbing, appliance, water-heater, freeze, vacancy, drainage, sump, sewer, septic, check-valve, and recurring-water-loss conditions to evidence review, corrective action, or referral when the source or repair status is unresolved.

Rule 220 requires referral for a requested water-backup limit above $25,000 and authorized approval for deductible handling, while an attached water-backup endorsement controls the contractual limit and deductible; the 2027-01 HO 04 90 endorsement states a $10,000 aggregate limit and a $1,000 deductible.

Rule 210's roof-age thresholds constrain underwriting eligibility rather than claim settlement; when attached and applicable, HO 23 74 2025-05 separately applies actual-cash-value treatment to covered roof surfacing at Roof Age 12 years or greater using reliable age evidence.

When Rule 220 water-exposure information is insufficient, the Manual prohibits binding until the missing information is obtained or authorized direction is recorded and requires a clear note of the condition, evidence, referral activity, and final action.

Rule 100 makes inspection currency and referral records part of the general underwriting lifecycle by treating an inspection report as current for 12 months after receipt, requiring resolution of material inspection concerns before final action, and requiring authorized approval conditions to be recorded.

Personal Lines Underwriting Manual Rule 700 requires every renewal file to be reviewed for changes affecting eligibility, exposure, valuation, occupancy, or loss potential, and requires material changes, unresolved underwriting conditions, and conflicting or unavailable information to be resolved or referred before renewal terms are released.

Rule 700 requires referral of a renewal risk with two paid property claims and directs review of loss cause, severity, recurrence, corrective action, open claims, and known circumstances that may lead to a claim; the claim-count threshold is an internal underwriting referral control rather than a policy limit.

Rule 700 treats an inspection report as valid for 12 months and requires updated information when it is no longer valid or conditions may have changed; conflicting inspection information must be reconciled before renewal terms are finalized.

Rule 700 identifies incomplete repairs, roof or exterior deterioration, water intrusion or repeated water damage, unsafe systems, vacancy or unoccupancy, changed occupancy or use, business or short-term rental activity, ownership changes, and material construction, valuation, protection, or hazard changes as renewal review or referral concerns.

Rule 700 requires a renewal outside assigned authority or relying on a continuing exception to have recorded current approval, and Rule 800 requires the referral or adverse-action file to preserve the basis, verified facts, authority response, approver, conditions, and final disposition.

Rule 800 requires the proposed transaction to be classified as cancellation, nonrenewal, withdrawal, or binding suspension, then requires policy-status verification, a supportable basis, verified information, jurisdiction review, approved reason language, correct policy and insured identification, approved delivery, and a hold when required facts or approval are missing.

Rule 800 contains internal instructions for a 10-day premium-default notice and a 45-day notice of intent not to renew, but those internal timing controls do not replace controlling state law, regulator requirements, or policy-form notice periods.

For the current New York position represented by DFS-2016-02 and HO 01 31 2016-04, nonrenewal requires at least 60 days before expiration, cancellation for a reason other than nonpayment requires at least 20 days, and nonpayment cancellation requires at least 15 days; notices require specific action, policy, effective-date, and reason information, and claims-based action requires relevant and verified claims information.

For Florida HO 01 09 2023-07, the contract form states 10 days for nonpayment cancellation, 45 days for another permitted cancellation, and 135 days for nonrenewal; separately, OIR-2023-04 requires at least 120 days and specific roof-related content for a roof-age or roof-condition nonrenewal, so the applicable policy edition, action type, and regulatory requirement must be checked rather than merged into one number.

Renewal and adverse-action files must retain the material facts and sources, loss and repair evidence, inspection review, referral and approval record, action classification, policy status, applicable jurisdiction and policy edition, timing analysis, notice version and content, delivery evidence, corrections, and final policy status.

Rules 500–570 are internal carrier underwriting controls for state-specific eligibility, authority, referrals, exceptions, and file documentation; they are not policy terms, coverage grants, or regulator bulletins.

A pending state-exception referral does not authorize binding: the underwriter must record the trigger, evidence, requested action, response, authority, conditions, and final disposition before completing the affected action.

Florida Rule 500 requires a roof inspection at age 15 or older, declines roofs at age 20 or older, sets Coverage A from $200,000 through $900,000, and limits line and senior authority to $600,000 and $900,000 respectively.

Florida Rule 500 refers repeated water, fire, liability, occupancy, business, animal, recreational, ground-movement, weather-loss, ownership, claims, maintenance, access, and inspection concerns, and requires state-exception support and complete file documentation for decisions.

Texas Rule 510 permits line authority through $800,000 Coverage A, sends amounts above that and through $1,200,000 to senior underwriting, declines or refers amounts above $1,200,000, refers water-backup limits above $25,000, and requires a roof inspection at age 15 or older.

Texas Rule 510 requires address, insurable-interest, occupancy, property, roof, loss, protective-device, system, deductible, and exception verification; it requires complete approval support before binding or declining and timely review for the applicable accept-or-deny deadline.

California Rule 520 sets a $1,000,000 line-underwriter ceiling, prohibits Coverage A above $2,000,000, requires 100% insured-to-value support for internal replacement-cost eligibility, and requires authorized direction for quake-deductible changes.

California Rule 520 refers unrepaired roof or fire damage, wildfire and vegetation hazards, open claims, nontraditional occupancy, construction, site instability, unsafe systems, protection gaps, material discrepancies, and unsupported mitigation; it requires a complete file for referrals, exceptions, and adverse decisions.
New York Rule 530 binds Coverage A through $750,000, requires referral for three paid property claims, and allows state-exception credits only when eligibility and support are confirmed.

New York Rule 530 refers unresolved damage, vacancy, lodging, business or agricultural use, unsafe premises and systems, recreational and animal hazards, occupancy and ownership conflicts, and requires underwriting direction before an intent-not-to-renew notice.

Louisiana Rule 540 declines roofs at age 20 or older, limits line authority to $500,000 Coverage A, sets a $750,000 Coverage A ceiling, and refers missing, conflicting, deteriorated, or incompletely repaired roof conditions.

Louisiana Rule 540 refers water, occupancy, business, recreational, animal, loss, claims, inspection, systems, drainage, flood, and backwater-valve concerns; it also refers unavailable maximum windstorm-and-hail deductible options, submissions outside the internal named-storm window, and unsupported exceptions while requiring final decision support.

North Carolina Rule 550 refers Coverage A above $700,000, requires a roof inspection at age 18 or older, refers changes to the fungi-and-bacteria aggregate, and refers requests exceeding the seacoast deductible ceiling.

North Carolina Rule 550 refers unresolved ownership, occupancy, construction, structural, loss, protection, access, coastal, water, hazard-material, valuation, and information issues, and requires authority-backed documentation for exception actions.

Colorado Rule 560 requires a roof inspection at age 12 or older, declines roofs at age 22 or older, requires review of the roof-schedule trigger age, refers Coverage A above $850,000 to appropriate authority, and refers wind deductibles above approved handling.

Colorado Rule 560 refers wildfire, vegetation, access, fire protection, heating and freeze, water, occupancy, business, animal, recreational, solar and energy-storage, structural, weather, construction, ownership, inspection, evidence, and protective-device concerns, and requires a complete file for referred or declined risks.

Illinois Rule 570 refers Coverage A above $700,000, water-backup limits above $15,000, and sewer-backup limits inconsistent with the described premises; it declines material application information that cannot be verified.

Illinois Rule 570 refers water, roof, systems, loss, occupancy, business, security, inspection, protected-class, consumer-reporting, exception, valuation, hazardous-storage, claim, and litigation concerns, prohibits protected-class underwriting, requires recorded exception approval, and requires a complete file.
Rules 500, 510, 520, 540, and 550 direct underwriters to use the rating manual’s state-exception pages as support for credits and to remove or refer unsupported or disputed credit treatment.
